RESULT v1 | k15d6b2f24a | A global lock is rejected because it forces every writer to serialize through one synchronous RPC round trip to a single coordinator, and at scale this becomes the concrete failure mode of a lock convoy: once request volume rises, the lock holder becomes a hot spot, any GC pause, network blip, or crash on that holder stalls every other client mid-RPC, and those clients retry in unison, producing a thundering herd of retries that saturates the coordinator's connection queue and drives cluster-wide latency into cascading timeouts, effectively a self-inflicted denial of service triggered by ordinary load rather than an external attacker. Instead of a global lock, the key-value store uses per-key optimistic concurrency control implemented as compare-and-swap on a version number attached to each record, so a writer reads the current value and version, computes its update locally, and submits the write only if the version still matches, letting the store reject stale writes with a single cheap check instead of holding a lock across the entire read-modify-write cycle, which removes the single coordination bottleneck and lets unrelated keys proceed fully in parallel. The tradeoff is that this scheme provides no cross-key atomicity: a transaction touching multiple keys can no longer be wrapped in one lock, so clients must detect CAS failures via version mismatch and retry the operation themselves, and under heavy contention on the same hot key, repeated retries substitute for the blocking a lock would have imposed, meaning the system trades strong multi-key transactional guarantees and simplicity of client code for higher availability and horizontal scalability under load.

RESULT v1 | k73afd345a7 | Matrix multiplication A x B = C for n x n matrices is expressed as an arithmetic circuit with n^3 multiplication gates and n^2 accumulation sums, and both R1CS and AIR formulations reduce this to rank-one and polynomial boundary constraints respectively. In R1CS, each partial product A[i][k] times B[k][j] becomes a rank-one constraint (L·w)(R·w) = O·w over witness vector w, giving n^3 such constraints, while the n^2 running sums are linear combinations folded into the O vector at zero additional multiplicative cost. In the AIR formulation used by STARK provers, the execution trace is a table indexed by row t corresponding to the triple (i, j, k) with i, j in zero to n-1 and k in zero to n-1, holding columns A_col, B_col, and an accumulator column acc. The transition constraint enforces acc(t) minus acc(t-1) minus A_col(t) times B_col(t) equals zero for every non-boundary row, a degree-2 polynomial identity checked over the trace domain via the composition polynomial and quotiented by the vanishing polynomial of that domain. Boundary constraints fix acc at k=0 to A[i][0] times B[0][j], and fix acc at k=n-1 to the target output C[i][j], for every (i,j) block of n rows, giving n^2 boundary pairs total across a trace of length n^3. This inner product accumulation pattern, one multiply-accumulate per row with boundary checks only at block edges, is what lets the prover commit once via FRI to a trace of degree n^3 rather than proving each of the n^3 multiplications as a separate constraint, yielding verifiable A x B = C with soundness reducible to the low-degree test on acc and the two boundary polynomials per output entry.

Inference is the third and final stage, in which the finetuned checkpoint is frozen, no further weight updates occur, and the model is deployed in a serving environment to generate outputs in response to new, live inputs. The boundary between pretraining and finetuning occurs when the base checkpoint is saved and then reloaded as the starting point for further training, and the boundary between finetuning and inference occurs when the weights are frozen and the model transitions from a training environment to a serving environment. In short, the fixed sequence is pretraining, then finetuning, then inference, with no stage able to begin before the artifact of the previous stage exists.
